title: Anyons and Inherently Complex F-symbols
authors: Matthew Buican, Peter Huston, Jiannis K. Pachos
abstract: Anyons in $2+1$ dimensions are not only characterized by exotic braiding statistics but also by intricate fusion properties. Two anyons may fuse into multiple topological charge sectors, and associativity of fusing three anyons to produce a fixed charge sector is governed by $F$-symbols. While braiding invariants, such as the modular data, are typically complex valued, a complete description of general anyon models requires understanding the arithmetic properties of its fusion associativity data as well. The $F$-symbols for many of the most common $2+1$d topological orders, including all Abelian anyon models as well as Fibonacci and Ising anyons, can be made real valued. We show this phenomenon is not universal by exhibiting braided fusion categories whose $F$-symbols cannot be made real. We call such $F$-symbols \lq\lq inherently complex." The examples we study lack a charge-conjugation symmetry and our results are therefore consistent with the converse of a statement proved in a companion work linking real $F$-symbols in braided fusion categories with the existence of a suitable charge-conjugation symmetry. We analyse the smallest-rank braided fusion categories we know of with inherently complex $F$-symbols: ${\rm Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_7\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_3)$ and ${\rm Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_4)$. Consequently, the corresponding $\mathcal Z({\rm Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_7\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_3))$ and $\mathcal Z({\rm Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_4))$ anyon models also have inherently complex $F$-symbols. Our presentation connects these examples with recent results on classifying anyons beyond modular data.
summary: This theoretical paper investigates the mathematical constraints on anyon models in 2+1 dimensions, focusing on the associativity data encoded in F-symbols. The authors prove that these symbols can be 'inherently complex'—meaning their non-real phases are unavoidable—by analyzing specific group representation categories lacking charge-conjugation symmetry. This deepens our understanding of topological order beyond simple braiding statistics.
main_problem: The central question is whether the associativity data (F-symbols) governing anyon fusion rules must be real-valued, or if they can possess inherent complex phases.
main_result: The authors demonstrate that inherently complex F-symbols do exist in unitary premodular categories, exemplified by $	ext{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_7times\mathbb{Z}_3)$ and $	ext{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5times\mathbb{Z}_4)$.
method: The analysis involves calculating gauge-invariant quantities built from F-symbols using representation theory techniques applied to specific group extensions, comparing them against known symmetries like charge-conjugation.
model_or_system: The study concerns anyons in $2+1$ dimensions, mathematically modeled by unitary braided spherical fusion categories (UMTCs), specifically analyzing the representations of semidirect products of cyclic groups ($	ext{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_n times \mathbb{Z}_m)$).
key_observables: F-symbols ($\mathcal{F}$), R-symbols, and derived gauge-invariant quantities whose non-real nature proves inherent complexity.
important_parameters: The structure of the underlying group extensions (e.g., $\mathbb{Z}_7times\mathbb{Z}_3$), which dictates the fusion rules and symmetry properties.
main_assumptions: The results are consistent with the converse of a statement linking real F-symbols to the existence of a charge-conjugation symmetry, and the examples studied lack this symmetry.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the definitions of F- and R-symbols, showing how they govern associativity (trivalent vertices) and braiding in the topological model.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing that modular data is insufficient for full classification, then develops methods to test for inherent complexity using tailored invariants, culminating in explicit calculations for specific group representations ($	ext{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_7times\mathbb{Z}_3)$ and $	ext{Rep}(\mathbb{Z}_5times\mathbb{Z}_4)$) that yield complex results.
why_interesting: This work pushes the boundaries of topological quantum field theory by showing that simple invariants (like modular data) are insufficient, requiring deeper analysis of fusion associativity structures for a complete physical description.
